lines.text: Bring back that same badly ordered struct from before, the one whose fields left real gaps between them.
Nothing in the language ever promised those gaps hold any particular value. Treating one of them as part of a real value is simply not allowed.
Take that exact struct, add one line asking a checked view to trust it, and ask the compiler to build it.
Does the compiler allow it?
Even when the structure still has those same gaps in it?
No. It refuses outright, and it refuses while building, not while running.

That's a fundamentally different kind of guarantee from a check that only fires if that exact line of code happens to execute. This one is proven about the shape of the type itself, once, before anything runs at all.
Switch to the earlier field order instead, the one with no gaps anywhere, and point a checked view straight at a raw buffer of bytes.
Every field comes back correct, and there isn't a single unsafe block written anywhere to make that happen.
Go back and actually try building that first, badly ordered struct with a checked view attached.
The compiler doesn't just say no. It names the exact reason: those very gaps, called out by name, as the thing that makes this unsound.
That's a world apart from a comment that merely hopes nobody ever gets this wrong.
Take two raw bytes that arrived from somewhere else entirely, and read them back without ever deciding which byte order they're supposed to be in.
On this particular machine, what number comes out?

tolerated.line: Take two raw bytes that arrived from somewhere else entirely, and read them back without ever deciding which byte order they're supposed to be in.

lines.text: A different number than the one that's actually correct, because this machine quietly assumed its own, local ordering.
Nothing about those two bytes themselves says which order they're in. That decision belongs entirely to whoever sent them, never to whichever machine happens to be reading them back.
Read those same two bytes a second way, this time honoring the order the sender actually chose, and compare the two results side by side.
One reading matches what was actually sent. The other, the one that quietly trusted this machine's own habits, simply doesn't.
Nothing about the bytes changed between the two readings. Only the assumption did.
A struct's gaps are never a promise of anything, which is exactly why reading them blind is never allowed.
A checked view refuses the moment those gaps exist, and needs no unsafe code at all once they don't.
And whatever arrives from somewhere else still carries its own choice of byte order, a choice the reading code has to honor on purpose, never assume for free.
